notes.short: “Saul, Saul”: his name said twice, in earnest
notes.about: Saul falls to the ground and hears a voice call his name twice; in the next verse the speaker says He is Jesus. The doubled name is emphatic and fixes Saul's attention. It can also show earnest concern for the man who was persecuting Him.

figure.name: Epizeuxis
figure.means: an urgent, emphatic call that fixes Saul's attention

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse among the doubled names in Figures of Speech, where he says the figure draws special attention to the person and to the weight of the words. Barnes calls the address emphatic: the repeated name would fix his attention. Henry says the doubling shows Saul needed calling again and again, and the tender concern Jesus had for him.

cites.quote: Seven of these are used by God to man (four of which are in the Old Testament, and three in the New), the other three being used under other circumstances. When thus used, the figure calls special attention to the occasion or to the person, and to some solemn moment of importance in the action, or of significance in the words. ... Saul, Saul (Act 9:4).
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: A mode of address that is emphatic. The repetition of the name would fix his attention.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: The doubling of it, Saul, Saul, intimates, First, The deep sleep that Saul was in; he needed to be called again and again ... Secondly, The tender concern that the blessed Jesus had for him, and for his recovery. He speaks as one in earnest
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

notes.short: “His rightful place”: Judas's end, gently told
notes.about: The prayer does not say outright what became of Judas. Read of him, as is most natural, the closing words speak of the traitor's end with restraint: he abandoned the apostleship “to go to his rightful place.”

figure.name: Euphemism
figure.words: to go to his rightful place
figure.means: the end that awaited the traitor, spoken of in softened and guarded words that do not name it

original.note: In Luke's Greek the words read literally his own place; the word behind “rightful” is idios, one's own.

notes.evidence: Brown (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) calls the words a euphemistic or softened expression of the traitor's awful future, a place both destined for him and suited to him. E. H. Plumptre (Ellicott's Commentary) takes them most naturally of Judas and finds in them the reserve of one who could neither cherish hope for him nor pronounce the condemnation that belongs to God.
notes.limit: The writers differ on how much the words say: one hears in them the doom suited to the traitor, the other a reserve that leaves the sentence to God. Some take the words of the man chosen in Judas's place, going to his own place among the Twelve.

cites.quote: A euphemistic or softened expression of the awful future of the traitor, implying not only destined habitation but congenial element.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: some interpreters have referred the words to the disciple about to be chosen, “to go to his own place” in the company of the Twelve. If we connect them, as seems most natural, with Judas, we find in them the kind of reserve natural in one that could neither bring himself to cherish hope nor venture to pronounce the condemnation which belonged to the Searcher of hearts.
cites.read: StudyLight's transcription, in the MyBible module at github.com/batanus/bible-resources (commit 14a8b1a)

notes.short: “Ministry and apostleship”: one office, not two
notes.about: Two nouns joined by “and” can be read as one office: the ministry of an apostle, the very work Judas abandoned. The second word shows what kind of ministry is meant.

figure.name: Hendiadys
figure.means: one thing, the apostolic ministry: the office and work of an apostle

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Hendiadys and reads it as this apostolic ministry, with the stress on apostolic. Barnes calls the words a hendiadys, two words used for one thing, meaning the apostolic ministry. Calvin says the sense is plainer when expounded as the ministry of the apostleship, by a figure he calls hypallage.
notes.limit: One writer also says the second word is added to join the dignity of the office to its burden, and he gives the figure another name.

cites.at: Hendiadys, or Two for One: Nouns, p. 665
cites.quote: this ministry, yes-this apostolic ministry, with emphasis on the adjective “apostolic,” which is obtained by exchange for the noun.
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: This is an instance of the figure of speech hendiadys, when two words are used to express one thing. It means the apostolic ministry.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: Because the word ministry was base, he addeth apostleship, wherein there is greater dignity; although the sense shall be more plain if you expound it, “the ministry of the apostleship.” For the figure hypallage is common in the Scriptures.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

notes.short: God's hand and will, then His will and hand
notes.about: Verse 28 names God's hand and then His will. The prayer takes them up again in reverse: it first turns to His will, asking Him to consider their threats and give His servants boldness to speak, and then to His hand, stretched out to heal.

lines.words: They carried out what Your hand
and will had decided beforehand would happen.
And now, Lord, consider their threats, and enable Your servants to speak Your word with complete boldness,
as You stretch out Your hand to heal

notes.evidence: Jebb takes God's hand in verse 28 as His over-ruling power and His counsel as His pre-disposing wisdom, and says these two topics give the subject of the next stanza, which takes them up by an epanodos in the inverted order, first with an appeal to the wisdom or counsel of God.

cites.quote: “thy hand,” that is, thine over-ruling power; “thy counsel,” that is, thy pre-disposing wisdom. These two topics give the subject of the next stanza; in which, by an epanodos, they are taken up in the inverted order. First, an appeal is made to the wisdom or “counsel” of God
cites.read: the 1820 printing, in the scan at archive.org/details/sacredliterature00jebb

notes.short: No land and no child, around a double promise
notes.about: Abraham is given no inheritance, and he has no child: these stand at the ends. Between them is the promise, made to him and to his descendants.

lines.words: He gave him no inheritance here, not even a foot of ground.
But God promised to give possession of the land to Abraham
even though he did not yet have a child.

notes.evidence: Boys sets out the verse in four lines: a double obstacle in the first and last, and a double promise in the two between.

cites.quote: In a. and a., a double obstacle; in b. and b., a double promise
cites.read: the 1824 printing, in the scan at archive.org/details/tactica-sacra

notes.short: Stephen breaks off in a cry of sharp rebuke
notes.about: Stephen's calm account of Israel's history breaks off in a cry: “You stiff-necked people with uncircumcised hearts and ears!” It is a sharp rebuke, and many read it as spoken when the council would no longer listen. Yet he dies praying for them: “Lord, do not hold this sin against them.”

figure.name: Exclamation
figure.words: You stiff-necked people with uncircumcised hearts and ears!
figure.means: Stephen's sharp rebuke and holy indignation, as he breaks off his speech

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists Acts 7:51 under Ecphonesis, words that burst out from feeling. Henry thinks it likely Stephen saw they would silence him, so he broke off and sharply rebuked them. Calvin calls it a sharp reprehension in holy zeal, breaking off before deaf men. Plumptre (Ellicott's Commentary) sees a sudden change from calm argument to vehement indignation, as the council seemed past control.

cites.quote: So that Ecphonesis is an outburst of words, prompted by emotion, and is not used as though any reply were expected. ... Act 7:51 is also an Ecphonesis.
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: It is probable that he perceived this, and that they were going to silence him; and therefore he breaks off abruptly in the midst of his discourse, and by that spirit of wisdom, courage, and power, wherewith he was filled, he sharply rebuked his persecutors, and exposed their true character
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: And he is enforced to use a sharp reprehension for a conclusion, Ye of an hard neck, saith he ... We see how soon he is offended with them with an holy zeal, but because he saw that he spake many things to small end, especially before deaf men, he breaketh off his doctrine.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: The sudden change of tone from calm argument to vehement indignation cannot be thought of as spontaneous. The excitement of the Sanhedrin, perhaps of the listening crowd also, at this point, would seem to have become uncontrollable.
cites.read: StudyLight's transcription, in the MyBible module at github.com/batanus/bible-resources (commit 14a8b1a)

notes.about: Paul has just called the church of God a flock (verse 28). Now he warns that savage wolves will come in among them, but does not say who they are. Many read them as false teachers who would prey on the church as wolves prey on sheep.

figure.name: Hypocatastasis
figure.means: false teachers who would come in and prey on the church, the flock

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Hypocatastasis, telling by implication what some who came after the apostle would be. Barnes says the wolves are false, hypocritical and dangerous teachers; Clarke, men professing to be teachers; Henry, seducers and false teachers; Brown (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown), teachers who would make a prey of the flock.
notes.limit: Some have taken the wolves to be persecutors; one writer gives that view and prefers false teachers. One writer also reads the verse as showing what kind of men would follow after the apostles.

cites.quote: “I know this, that after my departing shall grievous wolves enter in among you, not sparing the flock.” Thus does the Holy Spirit inform us, by Implication, as to the true character of “apostolic succession,” in order to impress the solemn fact on our minds.
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: Grievous wolves - Heavy βαρεῖς bareis, strong, mighty, dangerous wolves - so strong that the feeble flock would not be able to resist them. The term "wolves" is used to denote "the enemies of the flock - false, and hypocritical, and dangerous teachers."
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: Grievous wolves - Persons professing to be teachers; Judaizing Christians, who, instead of feeding the flock, would feed themselves, even to the oppression and ruin of the Church.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: Some understand it of persecutors ... It is rather to be understood of seducers and false teachers. ... these he calls grievous wolves, for though they came in sheep's clothing, nay, in shepherds' clothing, they made mischief in the congregations of Christians
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: both were to be teachers, but the one, "grievous wolves," not sparing, that is, making a prey of the flock
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: A saying of the Lord: giving is more blessed
notes.about: Paul ends his charge to the elders of Ephesus with a short saying of the Lord Jesus that is not written in the four Gospels: the giver is more blessed than the one who receives. He tells them to remember it as the reason to work hard and help the weak.

figure.name: Proverb
figure.part: Appear for the first time in Scripture
figure.words: It is more blessed to give than to receive
figure.means: the giver is more blessed than the one who receives, so the elders should work hard to help the weak

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Parœmia, or Proverb, among sayings that appear for the first time in Scripture and have since passed into general use, and calls it one of the un-recorded Parœmiœ or Logia of Christ.
notes.limit: The saying is the Lord's own, first written down here; the note does not claim it was a common proverb before He spoke it.

cites.at: Parœmiœ which appear for the first time in Scripture, p. 764
cites.quote: Parœmiœ which appear for the first time in Scripture; but, which, owing to their fulness of meaning and their wide application, have since passed into general use as proverbial sayings ... This is one of the un-recorded Parœmiœ or Logia of Christ.
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

notes.short: An old saying: kicking against the goads
notes.about: The voice from heaven meets Saul with a well-known saying from farm life. An ox that kicks back at the goad only drives the point in deeper. So Saul, in fighting against the Lord, was only hurting himself.

figure.name: Proverb
figure.part: Very probably already in use as proverbial expressions
figure.words: It is hard for you to kick against the goads
figure.means: fighting against the Lord is as useless as an ox kicking the goad: it only hurts the one who kicks

original.note: In Luke's Greek the goads are kentra, iron-pointed sticks used to drive oxen at the plough.

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists it under Parœmia, or Proverb, as common among Greeks and Hebrews. In their notes on the same words at Acts 9:5, Albert Barnes and Adam Clarke call it a proverbial expression, E. H. Plumptre (Ellicott's Commentary) one of the oldest Greek proverbs, and John Calvin a proverbial sentence drawn from goaded oxen or horses.
notes.limit: Several of the writers find the saying among the Greeks. One says it was common among the Hebrews too; another finds it in no collection of Hebrew proverbs. In the BSB the saying stands here, in Paul's own account, and not at Acts 9:5.

cites.at: Parœmiœ which, though not quoted as such, were very probably already in use as proverbial expressions, p. 760
cites.quote: This was a proverb common among the Greeks as well as the Hebrews.
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: This is evidently a proverbial expression. ... The expression "to kick against the prick" is derived from the action of a stubborn and unyielding ox kicking against the goad. And as the ox would injure no one by it but himself
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: This is a proverbial expression, which exists, not only in substance, but even in so many words, both in the Greek and Latin writers. Κεντρον, kentron, signifies an ox goad, a piece of pointed iron stuck in the end of a stick, with which the ox is urged on when drawing the plough.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: This is a proverbial sentence, taken from oxen or horses, which, when they are pricked with goads, do themselves no good by kicking, save only that they double the evil by causing the prick to go farther into their skins.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: In their outward form they were among the oldest and most familiar of Greek proverbs. ... They do not occur in any collection of Hebrew proverbs ... What they taught was, of course, that to resist a power altogether superior to our own is a profitless and perilous experiment.
cites.read: StudyLight's transcription, in the MyBible module at github.com/batanus/bible-resources (commit 14a8b1a)
